title: Modals, Part 1

items.fix: Applicants must fill in the forms in ink.

items.fix: We've got to finish this project before we go home tonight.

items.title: Modals add an attitude
lines: They show: necessary, a good idea, possible, allowed.

items.title: Two iron rules
lines: No s, ever. Then the simple verb. No to.

items.text: Applicants ___ the forms in ink.
items.why: modal + simple verb. No to, no s.

items.title: One exception: ought to
lines: ought always keeps its to.
chips: He ought to go to the meeting.

items.title: Phrasal modals
lines: Longer cousins with the same meaning. They use to.
items.tip: These DO change: she has to, he is able to, they are supposed to.

items.text: A teacher ___ give homework.
items.why: After doesn't → simple form: have to.

lines: Modal + simple verb. No -s, no to: She can do it.
Exception: ought to. Phrasal modals: have to, be able to, be supposed to.

examples.text: She can do it.
He ought to go to the meeting.
School can be stressful.

items.text: School can be stressful.
Too much work may be harm a student's health.
items.why: may + one simple verb: may harm.
items.fix: Too much work may harm a student's health.

items.text: A teacher doesn't has to give homework.
items.fix: A teacher doesn't have to give homework.

items.text: Science and math might be the two most important skills for the future.

She cans do it.

items.why: can is a modal: she can.
It changes: she is able to.
must is a modal: he must.
It changes: we are supposed to.
It changes: she has got to.

levels.title: No choice
levels.full: Expressing Necessity: Must, Have To, Have Got To

items.title: It is necessary
lines: must = have to = have got to.
There is no other choice.

examples.text: All applicants must take an entrance exam.
All applicants have to take an entrance exam.

items.title: Which one, where?

examples.text: Cell phones must be in your backpacks during class.
Johnny, you must stay away from the stove.
I have to go to a business meeting at 1:00.
He has to go to a meeting tonight.

items.tip: In conversation, people say have to much more than must.

items.text: Sorry. Julie and I ___ leave the party early. (two friends talking)

items.title: have got to = gotta
lines: Informal, spoken. Same meaning.
chips: I have got to go now.
items.tip: In writing, keep have: I've got to go. Not: I got to go.

items.title: Questions use have to
lines: Do you have to…? Does she have to…?
chips: Does Vicki have to work tomorrow?

items.text: ___ work tomorrow?

lines: must / have to / have got to = necessary. No choice.
must: rules and signs. have to: everyday. Questions: Do you have to…?

examples.text: All applicants must take an entrance exam.
I have to go to a meeting at 1:00.
I've got to go now.

items.text: Oh, gosh. Look at the time. I've got to go. I have class in five minutes!
All applicants must be 18 years of age and must have a valid driver's license.
We have to prepare a research paper in Dr. Chen's seminar this term.
items.why: have to is the everyday choice.

items.text: A rule about documents
options: Your signature on the document has to be legible.
Your signature on the document must be legible.

items.text: Friends going to a movie
options: We've got to hurry. The movie starts in ten minutes.
We must hurry. The movie starts in ten minutes.

items.text: Talking about friends on the road
options: They have to stop for gas.

items.text: A driving rule
options: Drivers have got to renew their licenses in person.
Drivers must renew their licenses in person.

items.text: All passengers ___ show their passports to the customs officer.
Mai ___ get up early tomorrow.
Sorry. Julie and I ___ leave the party early.

I'll be home a little late. I ___ pick up groceries after work.
___ work tomorrow?
Drivers ___ pull over when they see a police car's flashing lights.
___ play his music so loud every night?

items.why: An adult giving a child a rule → must.

items.text: ___ buy our tickets in advance?
What ___ after class today?
What ___ first thing in the morning?
What time ___ in your first class?
What are some rules that students ___ follow?
People say “I hafta be home by eight.” They mean…
options: I have to be home by eight.
I had to be home by eight.

items.text: People say “I gotta go.” In writing, it is…
items.why: Keep have in writing: I've got to go.

items.text: He ___ go to a meeting tonight.

talk.title: What do you have to do?
talk.task: Claude asks about your duties today and the rules at your school or job.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Ask me one question at a time: What do you have to do after class or work today? What do you have to do first thing in the morning? What time do you have to be at your first class or at work? What are some rules that students or employees must follow? I answer with have to / have got to for my everyday duties and must for rules. Check the forms (has to with he/she, no 'to' after must).

levels.title: Not needed vs. forbidden
levels.full: Lack of Necessity (Not Have To) and Prohibition (Must Not)

lesson.title: Learn: don't have to vs. must not

items.title: Same meaning, opposite negatives
lines: must = have to.
But must not ≠ don't have to!

items.title: Relax, or stop?

examples.text: Tomorrow is a holiday. We don't have to go to class.
I can hear you. You don't have to shout.
You must not tell anyone my secret.

items.tip: don't have to: you can if you want. must not: no choice. It's forbidden.

items.text: The meeting starts in an hour. We have plenty of time. We ___ hurry.
items.why: No need to hurry → don't have to.

items.text: Patients ___ leave the hospital without their doctor's permission.

items.title: Softer ways to forbid
lines: must not is very strong. People often say:
chips: You can't tell anyone my secret.
You'd better not tell anyone my secret.

lines: don't have to = not necessary (you can if you want).
must not = forbidden. Don't do it!

examples.text: We don't have to go to class tomorrow.
You must not tell anyone my secret.

items.text: The meeting starts in an hour. We have plenty of time.
items.why: No need → don't have to / don't need to.
items.ask: Tick the answers that make sense

items.text: You ___ skip class. Unexcused absences will lower your grade.
items.why: It's against the rules → must not.

items.text: I ___ contact my professor. I found the information I was looking for.
items.why: Not necessary now → don't have to.

items.text: I ___ go to the doctor. I'm feeling much better.
Patients ___ leave the hospital without their doctor's permission.
You ___ introduce me to your doctor. We've already met.
Park visitors ___ approach the bears. They can be dangerous.
If you encounter a bear, you ___ run. Instead, back away slowly.
A person ___ get married in order to lead a happy life.
A person ___ become rich and famous in order to live a successful life.
We've got to buy groceries on the way home. → We ___ groceries on the way home.
items.why: Negative of have (got) to → don't have to.

items.text: You have to wait for Martha. → You ___ for Martha.
The city has got to offer more public transportation. → The city ___ more options.
items.why: The city = it → doesn't have to.

items.text: You must fill out the form by tomorrow. → You ___ the form by tomorrow.
items.why: Not necessary → don't have to (not must not).

items.text: Jin has to work overtime this weekend. → Jin ___ overtime this weekend.
An effective leader ___ use his or her power for personal financial gain.
items.why: That is wrong and forbidden → must not.

items.text: An effective leader ___ ignore the wishes of the majority of the people.
items.why: A leader should never do it → must not.

items.text: An effective leader ___ be wealthy.
An effective leader ___ be male.
Don't carry large sums of money with you.
options: You don't have to carry large sums of money.
You must not carry large sums of money.

items.text: The guide said it's not necessary to rent a car. There is a bus.
options: You don't have to rent a car.
You must not rent a car.

items.text: To apply for a visa, proof of citizenship is necessary.
options: You must show proof of citizenship.
You have to show proof of citizenship.
You should show proof of citizenship.
items.ask: Tick all with the same meaning

items.text: It will be a good idea to arrive at the train station early tomorrow.
items.why: A good idea = should / ought to.
items.ask: Tick all with the same meaning

items.text: Only airline passengers with boarding passes can go to the gate.
options: To go to the gate, passengers should have boarding passes.
To go to the gate, passengers must have boarding passes.

items.text: “You'd better not tell anyone my secret.”
“You can't tell anyone my secret.”
items.why: can't here = it is not allowed.

talk.title: A good leader
talk.task: What must a good leader do, and what doesn't a leader have to be? Tell Claude.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Ask me about an effective leader of a country, one quality at a time: be well educated / be flexible and open to new ideas / be wealthy / have a family / have a military background / use power for personal financial gain / ignore the wishes of the majority / be a good public speaker. For each, I say: An effective leader must ..., must not ..., has to ..., or doesn't have to ..., and give a short reason. Check that I use must not for prohibition and doesn't have to for lack of necessity.

levels.title: Good advice
levels.full: Advisability/Suggestions: Should, Ought To, Had Better, Could

lesson.title: Learn: should, ought to, had better, could

items.title: should = ought to
lines: This is a good idea. This is my advice.

examples.text: You should study harder.
You ought to study harder.

items.tip: Negative: shouldn't. (ought to is rare in the negative.)

items.title: had better = or else!
lines: Stronger. A warning about a bad result.
chips: We had better stop at the next gas station. (or we'll run out of gas)
You'd better take care of that cut.
items.tip: Form: had better + simple verb. It talks about now or the future, not the past.

items.text: The gas tank is almost empty. We ___ stop at the next gas station.
items.why: had better + simple verb. No to.

items.title: should vs. could

examples.text: You should talk to your teacher.
You could talk to your teacher.
Or you could ask Ann to help you.

items.tip: Softer still: Maybe you should… / You might want to… / I would…

items.text: “He could call his doctor. Or he could postpone his trip.” The speaker is…
items.why: could = possibilities, not one firm answer.

lines: should / ought to = a good idea. had better = a warning (or else…).
could = one possible idea. had better + simple verb, no to.

examples.text: You should study harder.
We had better stop at the next gas station.
You could talk to your teacher.

items.text: Amir has a bad toothache.
options: He should get a friend to pull the tooth right away.
items.why: A dentist is the sensible advice.

items.text: The shoes I bought last week don't fit. I've only worn them indoors.
options: You should take them back to the store.
You had better wear them every day.

items.text: Flights fill up fast near the holidays. I haven't gotten my ticket yet.
options: You could wait a few more months.
You'd better buy your ticket soon.
items.why: A warning: or there will be no seats.

items.text: Yikes! My class starts in five minutes.
options: You ought to take a nap.
items.why: Or you will be late → You'd better hurry.

items.text: I have the hiccups.
options: You could drink a glass of water.

items.text: I bought these expensive apples, and all of them are rotten inside.
options: You ought to take them back and ask for a refund.
items.why: A good idea → ought to take them back.

items.text: I have six months to improve my English.
options: You should practice a little every day.

items.text: Ted feels sick and has a flight tomorrow. “He should go to urgent care right now.”
items.why: should = this is what I recommend.

items.text: “Well, he could call his doctor for advice. Or he could postpone his trip.”
“You should take the airport shuttle. It's cheaper than a taxi.”
“You could take the shuttle. Maybe you could ask Matt to drive you.”
You ___ take care of that cut on your hand soon, or it will get infected.
items.why: A bad result is coming → had better.

items.text: You'd better ___ late.
I ___ study tonight, but I think I'll watch TV instead.
You ___ leave your keys in the car.
A person ___ eat in order to live.
items.why: It is necessary to stay alive → has to.

items.text: A person ___ eat a balanced diet.
The weather is so gloomy. Maybe we ___ go somewhere warm for our vacation.
An incoming freshman ___ have four years of high school English. Three is not enough.
If you want to become a doctor, you ___ go to medical school for many years.
items.why: There is no other way → have to.

items.text: I don't have enough money to take the bus, so I ___ walk home.
If you want to get more exercise, you ___ walk to and from work.
Rice ___ have water in order to grow.
“I think you should be more direct.”
“There are a few ways you could handle this.”
options: You must do all of them.

items.text: “You might want to sit down with her and say…”
items.why: might want to = a soft suggestion.

items.text: “You could tell her that all her stuff has to be on her side of the line.”
“If she won't make any changes, I would talk to a dorm advisor.”
options: If I were you, I'd do this.
I talked to an advisor last year.
items.why: I would… = advice: if I were you.

items.text: Which is the softest advice?
options: You had better talk to her.
Maybe you could talk to her.

talk.title: Dear Claude, I need advice
talk.task: Invent a small problem. Claude gives advice. Then you give advice for Claude's problem.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. First ask me to describe a small personal problem (real or invented), like a messy roommate. Give me short advice using should, could and had better. Then tell me one problem of your own and ask for my advice. I must use should / ought to / had better / could. Check the forms (had better + simple verb, no 'to' after should).

talk.title: Oops!
talk.task: Claude has little accidents. Tell Claude what to do: “You'd better…”, “You could…”.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Tell me one small problem at a time: Oops! I spilled coffee on my shirt. / My boss is coming for dinner and I'm a terrible cook. / I've been studying for three days straight. / My apartment is a mess and my mother is coming tomorrow. I answer with advice using You'd better ..., You should ..., or Maybe you could .... Check the forms.

items.title: Someone expects it
lines: am / is / are supposed to + verb.
A plan, a rule, or good manners.
chips: The game is supposed to begin at 10:00. (schedule)
The committee is supposed to vote by secret ballot. (correct way)
The children are supposed to put away their toys. (behavior)

items.text: We ___ bring our books to class every day.

items.title: I am supposed to ≠ I suppose
lines: I am supposed to go = people expect me to go.
I suppose = I guess.
chips: I am supposed to go to the meeting. My boss wants me there.

items.title: should = I expect it soon
lines: should can mean “I think it will happen”.
chips: The mail should be here soon.
Amy should be back any minute.

items.text: It's 10:00. I expect the movie is over now. = The movie ___ over now.

lines: be supposed to = someone expects it (schedule, rule, manners).
should can also mean: I expect it to happen.

examples.text: The game is supposed to begin at 10:00.
Amy should be back any minute.

missions.title: What are you supposed to do?

items.text: In my country, students ___ stand up when a teacher enters the room.
If a traffic light turns red, you ___ come to a complete stop.
The game ___ begin at 10:00.
items.why: The game = it → is supposed to.

items.text: What time ___ be at the train station tomorrow?
The janitor ___ unlock the building doors.
items.why: The janitor = he → is supposed to.

items.text: I am supposed to go to the meeting.
items.why: am supposed to = am expected to.

items.text: Athletes in training ___ stay up all night.
I expect the movie is over now. → The movie ___ over now.
I expect Aja will hear about the job offer soon. → Aja ___ about the job offer soon.
I expect your advisor will have a solution for you. → Your advisor ___ a solution for you.
I expect our flight will take off on time. → Our flight ___ on time.
I expect the mail will be here soon. → The mail ___ here soon.
The teacher should be back any minute. She just needed to get supplies.
options: I expect she will be back very soon.
She has a duty to come back.

items.text: Seat belt (1)
options: You had better wear a seat belt.
You have to wear a seat belt.

items.text: Seat belt (2)
options: You must wear a seat belt.
You had better wear a seat belt.

items.text: Seat belt (3)
options: You have to wear a seat belt.
You are supposed to wear a seat belt.
items.why: have to is stronger than an expectation.

items.text: ID (1)
options: We are supposed to bring ID.

items.text: ID (2)
options: We have got to bring ID.

items.text: ID (3)
items.why: should (advice) is stronger than could (an idea).

talk.title: Jobs and duties
talk.task: What should a nurse, a taxi driver or a tour guide do? What must they not do?
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Name one job at a time (a tour guide, an artist, an engineer, a nurse, a taxi driver, a salesclerk, a plumber, a vet). I make two or three sentences about it using should, have to, be supposed to, must, must not, doesn't have to, had better not (for example: A vet should be very gentle with animals.). Check my modal forms.

talk.title: Customs in my country
talk.task: What are people supposed to do in your country (shoes, greetings, classrooms)?
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Ask me one question at a time about customs in my country: Are people supposed to take off their shoes before they enter a home? Are students supposed to stand up when a teacher enters? How are children supposed to address adults? What are you supposed to do if you are involved in a traffic accident? I answer with be (not) supposed to. Check the form: am/is/are + supposed + to.

levels.title: I can do it
levels.full: Ability: Can, Know How To, and Be Able To

lesson.title: Learn: can, know how to, be able to

items.title: can = ability
lines: Body power, or the five senses.
chips: Tom is strong. He can lift that heavy box.
I can see Central Park from my apartment.

items.title: Learned skills: know how to
lines: You learned it? Both work.
chips: Maria knows how to play the piano.

items.text: Larry ___ start a fire without matches. He learned it at camp.

items.title: be able to = can
lines: Same meaning. It changes with the subject.
chips: I am able to help you now.
Are you able to help me?
Sorry, I'm not able to help you.
Sorry, I'm unable to help you.

items.text: I ___ help you. I don't have training in this area.

items.title: Hearing can and can't
lines: can is weak and fast: “kn”. can't is strong and clear.
chips: My mother can't speak English well.

lines: can = ability. can / know how to = a learned skill.
be able to = can: I am able to help. I'm not able to help.

examples.text: He can lift that heavy box.
Maria knows how to play the piano.
I am able to help you now.

items.text: Isabel knows how to play chess.
Jonathan can run really fast. He's a natural.
Theodore knows how to use sign language. His mother taught him.
I won't be able to go swimming on our trip. I have an ear infection.
items.why: The body can't do it now.

items.text: Tom is strong. He ___ that heavy box.
My husband ___ awake past 10:00.
Maria ___ the piano. She's been taking lessons for years.
Sorry, I'm ___ help you. It's too heavy.

missions.title: Say it with be able to

items.text: Larry can start a fire without matches. → Larry ___ a fire without matches.
I can't send a text. I left my phone at home. → I ___ a text.
Can you read the doctor's handwriting? → ___ the doctor's handwriting?
Thomas can't drive without glasses. → Thomas ___ without glasses.
I can't remove the stain on your white shirt. → I ___ the stain.
Every employee can do CPR. → Every employee ___ CPR.
Larry can start a fire without matches.
options: Yes: Larry knows how to start a fire.
items.why: A learned skill → know how to works.
items.ask: Can you say it with know how to?

items.text: I can't send a text. I left my phone at home.
options: No: it's not about a skill.
items.why: The problem is the phone, not the skill.
items.ask: Can you say it with know how to?

items.text: Every employee can do CPR.
options: Yes: Every employee knows how to do CPR.
items.ask: Can you say it with know how to?

items.say: We can come to the meeting.
Our two-year-old can count to fifty.
You can't take that course next term.

talk.title: Sleep habits
talk.task: Claude asks about your sleep: Are you able to fall asleep easily? Can you sleep on airplanes?
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Ask me one question at a time about my sleep habits: In general, are you able to fall asleep easily? How many hours can you sleep before waking up? Are you able to function well with less sleep? Are you able to sleep with noise? Can you sleep on airplanes? Do you know how to recover from jet lag quickly? I answer in full sentences with can / can't / am (not) able to / know how to. Check the forms.

items.title: Two kinds of “possible”

examples.text: Spices can be expensive.
You can learn a lot by watching cooking shows.

right.label: may / might: a chance, this time

examples.text: Spices may be more expensive at that store.
Liza might need your help in the kitchen.

items.tip: may = might here. Both mean: there is a chance.

items.text: Pepper ___ make people sneeze. (a general fact)

items.title: Not can for one chance
lines: One real situation, now or tomorrow? Use may / might.

items.text: There is a 50% chance. It ___ snow tomorrow night.
This apartment sounds nice, but it ___ be too far away from my job.

lines: can = generally possible: Spices can be expensive.
may / might = there is a chance now or later: It might snow.

examples.text: Spices can be expensive.
It might snow tomorrow night.

items.text: This soup may need salt and pepper.
options: A chance now or in the future
items.why: This soup, right now → a chance.

items.text: Pepper can make people sneeze.
options: A chance now or in the future

items.text: Spices can make food taste better.
options: A chance now or in the future

items.text: My cooking tonight might be too spicy for you.
options: A chance now or in the future

items.text: Physical exercise can improve your mental state.
items.why: A general possibility → can is fine.

items.text: The weather may be breezy tomorrow.
The weather can be breezy tomorrow.
items.why: One future chance → may / might, not can.
items.fix: The weather may be breezy tomorrow.

items.text: Eating out every day can be expensive.
The apartment sounds nice, but it can be too far away from my job.
items.fix: The apartment sounds nice, but it may be too far away from my job.

items.text: Eating out every day might be expensive for you.
items.why: A chance for one person → might.

items.text: Freshman year CAN turn out to be the most challenging time in college.
One of the biggest differences is the amount of freedom you MUST learn to manage.
In high school, you generally CAN'T choose how you spend your day.
options: It is not possible / not allowed.

items.text: The class schedule MIGHT NOT be the same every day.
options: There is a chance it isn't.

items.text: You can sleep in one morning and HAVE TO be up early the next.
College professors DON'T HAVE TO take attendance.
Your grades MAY suffer if you can't manage time well.
With an understanding of the challenges ahead, you CAN prepare in advance.
items.why: can = it is possible for you.

items.text: Online courses ___ be convenient for busy people.
Take an umbrella. It ___ rain this afternoon.
People ___ learn a lot about life from traveling.
I'm not sure where Liza is. She ___ be in the kitchen.
Music ___ help you feel calmer tonight. Try it.
Too much sun ___ be dangerous.

talk.title: It can… / It might…
talk.task: Finish Claude's sentences: “Online courses can be…”, “Music might help us feel…”.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Give me one sentence starter at a time and ask me to finish it: Students may learn best ... / Online courses can be ... / Studying all classes online might be ... / People can learn a lot about life from ... / Music might help us feel ... / Literature may help us ... Check that I use can for general possibility and may/might for a chance.

talk.title: Managing your time
talk.task: What should a student do to manage time better? Give Claude 4 tips.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Ask me: What are some major distractions for students today? Has time management ever been a problem for you? Then ask me for four recommendations for a student who needs to manage time better. I must use should / should not / ought to / had better. Check the forms.

items.title: Two kinds of request
lines: May I…? = I want to do something.
Would you…? = I want YOU to do something.

items.title: I + May / Could / Can
lines: May I is the most formal. Can I is the most relaxed.
chips: May I borrow your pen, please?
Could I please borrow your pen?
items.tip: Could I…? is about now, not the past.

items.title: Asking you to do it
lines: Would you and Could you are the most polite.
chips: Would you pass the salt, please?
Will you please pass the salt?

items.text: ___ you help me?
items.why: May is only for I / we. → Could you…?

items.title: How to answer
lines: Say yes kindly. Saying no? Start with “I'd like to, but…”
chips: I'd like to, but I can't reach it.

items.text: Hello. ___ I help you?
items.why: With I → May / Could / Can. Not Would.

lines: I do it: May I / Could I / Can I…? You do it: Would you / Could you / Will you / Can you…?
Never: May you…?

examples.text: May I borrow your pen, please?
Would you pass the salt, please?

items.text: Excuse me, ___ I look at that book?
___ you hand me that book, please?
___ you pass the salt, please?
